images.title: Why most welcome sequences fail
images.alt: Comparison of failing affiliate welcome sequences with a short five-email sequence that delivers, helps, then makes one recommendation.
images.caption: A short sequence earns trust before it asks for anything.

columns.label: Sequences that fail
points: A pitch in the very first email
Selling to someone who joined an hour ago

columns.label: A sequence that works
points: Five emails over about ten days
Emails 2 and 3 are useful, nothing to sell

images.after: What the recommendation email looks like
images.title: What a good recommendation email does
images.alt: Checklist for an affiliate recommendation email: tie to a known problem, one product, who should skip it, disclosure before the link.
images.caption: It should read like advice from someone who knows the topic, not a sales page.

items: Ties back to a problem you already wrote about
Names one product and who it suits
Says plainly who should skip it
Puts the commission disclosure before the link
Only claims testing you actually did
Leaves out countdowns, "last chance" and bonus stacks

images.after: Keeping the sequence honest over time
images.title: A check-up every few months
images.alt: Steps to audit an automated email sequence: subscribe with a spare address, click every link, review email 4 clicks and drop-off, prune inactive subscribers.
images.caption: An automated sequence keeps sending whatever you wrote, so read it as a new subscriber would.

items.title: Subscribe with a spare address
items.text: Read the whole sequence the way a new subscriber would.

items.title: Click every link
items.text: Catch discontinued products and programs whose terms have changed.

items.title: Look at the numbers
items.text: Check clicks on email 4 and where opens fall off.

items.title: Change one thing at a time
items.text: That way you can tell what made the difference.

items.title: Ask quiet subscribers
items.text: Send one "do you still want these?" email and remove those who don't answer.
